title: Demo — Numerical Optimization & Linear Algebra (exam-eve notes)

notes.raw:
Numerical Optimization & Linear Algebra — exam-eve notes (messy, sorry)
Prof said 60% of the paper is Unit 3.
GRADIENT DESCENT (GD): minimize f(x) by moving against the gradient: x <- x - alpha * grad f(x). alpha = step size / learning rate. too big => oscillate/diverge, too small => crawl. Worked example from the slide: f(x)=x^2-2, f'(x)=2x, x0=3, alpha=0.1: x1=2.4, x2=1.92, x3=1.536 … creeps toward sqrt(2)=1.4142 but slowly (linear convergence).

NEWTON'S METHOD: x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k). From Taylor: f(x+p) ≈ f(x) + p f'(x) + 0.5 p^2 f''(x); minimize that quadratic model and p = -f/f'. In n-D: solve H p = -grad f (Hessian). Newton converges quadratically near the root. Half-derivation done in class: f=x^2-2, x0=3: f=7, f'=6, step -7/6 -> x1=1.8333; then f(1.8333)=1.3611, f'=3.6667 -> x2=1.4621 … lands on sqrt2 in 4 steps. DANGER: if f'(x) is small the jump goes anywhere (division by nearly nothing).

LINE SEARCH: instead of fixing alpha, pick it each round so f drops "enough" — Armijo rule: accept alpha if f(x - alpha g) <= f(x) - c*alpha*|g|^2 with c about 1e-4 (backtracking: halve alpha until true). One line on the slide, forgot the rest

QUASI-NEWTON / BFGS (pasted from slide, no intuition given): H_{k+1} = (I - rho s y^T) H_k (I - rho y s^T) + rho s s^T with rho = 1/(y^T s), s = x_{k+1} - x_k, y = g_{k+1} - g_k. H approximates the inverse Hessian, so p = -H g then line search. "secant condition" H y = s?? something about curvature. memorize or cry.

Eigen recap for symmetric matrices: A = Q Lambda Q^T, orthonormal eigenvectors in Q. Used everywhere in Unit 4 but I forgot the construction. Exam hinted "make the vectors perpendicular then unit" — ???? don't remember how.

syllabus.raw:
Unit 3 — Unconstrained Optimization
- Gradient descent
- Newton's method
- Line search (Armijo)
- Quasi-Newton methods (BFGS)
Unit 4 — Linear Algebra for optimization
- Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization
- Conjugate gradient

lesson.oneLiner: Guess a root, ride the tangent line to where it hits zero, repeat — converges quadratically.
lesson.why: It turns a hard nonlinear problem into a sequence of easy linear ones (solve f'·p = −f, or H·p = −∇f in n-D), and near the root each step roughly squares the error.
lesson.analogy: Like finding where a hillside path crosses the stream: at your spot you look at the slope of the ground right under your feet and walk to where that straight slope hits water.

steps.text: Iterate x − f(x)/f′(x) until x stops moving.
It comes from minimizing the Taylor quadratic model — p = −f/f′.
You must compute the derivative f′ each step (in n-D, solve H p = −grad).
Stop when |f(x)| is below your tolerance.

pitfalls.text: If f′(x) is small the step divides by nearly nothing and the jump goes anywhere.
Far from the root Newton can diverge or cycle — fall back to gradient descent or damp the step.
For systems you need the Hessian every iteration; that cost is exactly what quasi-Newton methods avoid.

notesGaps: No stopping criterion or tolerance is written down
No multi-dimensional worked example with a Hessian solve

trace.title: Newton on f(x)=x²−2 from x₀=3
narration: From x=3, with f=7 and f′=6, the tangent line hits zero at 1.8333.
At 1.8333 the residual dropped to 1.3611; the next Newton step gives 1.4621.
By 1.4621 the error is small — f is only 0.1378 and one more step reaches 1.415.
At 1.415, f=0.0022 and the step lands on 1.4142, right to 4 decimals.
trace.takeaway: Each step roughly squares the error — that is quadratic convergence.

lesson.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[guess x0] --> B[compute f and f-prime]
  B --> C[x = x - f / f-prime]
  C --> D{f small enough?}
  D -- no --> B
  D -- yes --> E[root found]

examQuestion.q: Use one Newton step to approximate the root of f(x)=x³−2 starting at x₀=1.5. State f and f′, give the numeric estimate, and say what convergence order you expect. (5 marks)

lesson.oneLiner: Skip the Hessian: keep updating a matrix H that behaves like the inverse Hessian, using only gradient differences.
lesson.why: Newton's method needs and factorizes the Hessian every step — expensive and sometimes unavailable. BFGS learns curvature from the vectors s (step) and y (gradient change) you already have, and keeps H positive definite so −H·g is always a descent direction.
lesson.analogy: Instead of surveying the hill with laser instruments every step, you carry a stretchy map that you bend once per step from what you just felt.

steps.text: Update H with the pasted formula: H₊ = (I−ρsyᵀ) H (I−ρysᵀ) + ρssᵀ, ρ = 1/(yᵀs).
s = x₊−x is the step taken; y = g₊−g is the gradient change.
Search along p = −H·g, since H approximates the inverse Hessian.
Line-search α along p (Armijo backtracking is enough).
Stop when ‖g‖ is tiny; superlinear convergence in practice.

pitfalls.text: The secant condition H·y = s only makes sense when yᵀs > 0 — it needs an Armijo/Wolfe line search, not a fixed step.
Don't store or invert the Hessian — the whole point is the cheap rank-2 update.
Start H₀ = I; a bad H₀ just costs the first couple of steps.

notesGaps: Why the update keeps H positive definite (the intuition the slide skipped)
How the Wolfe/Armijo conditions protect yᵀs > 0
No intuition for 'superlinear' vs Newton's quadratic rate

trace.title: BFGS on f(x)=x₁²+2x₂² from (4,1) with Armijo backtracking
narration: At x=(4, 1) with f=18 and gradient norm 8.9443, H is still the identity; the accepted step is 0.5.
The updated H=[[2, 0.5], [0.5, 1.25]] knows the valley shape: from (0, -1), f=2, a shorter step 0.25 is taken.
Now at (0.5, 0.25), f is down to 0.375, gradient norm 1.4142, step 0.125.
By (0.1065, -0.1713) f=0.07 and ‖grad‖=0.7175 — closing in without ever forming the Hessian.
trace.takeaway: Each rank-2 update teaches H the curvature the gradient change just revealed, so steps get sharper for free.

lesson.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[start x, H = identity] --> B[p = -H times grad]
  B --> C[Armijo line search along p]
  C --> D[s = new x - x, y = new g - g]
  D --> E[rank-2 BFGS update of H]
  E --> F{grad small?}
  F -- no --> B
  F -- yes --> G[done]

examQuestion.q: State the BFGS inverse-Hessian update and the secant condition it satisfies. Why must the line search keep yᵀs > 0? (6 marks)
examQuestion.modelAnswer:
H₊ = (I − ρ s yᵀ) H (I − ρ y sᵀ) + ρ s sᵀ, ρ = 1/(yᵀs), s = x₊−x, y = g₊−g.
It satisfies the secant condition H₊ y = s (curvature matching).
yᵀs > 0 is needed so ρ > 0 and the update keeps H positive definite, guaranteeing −H g is a descent direction; Armijo/Wolfe conditions enforce it.

lesson.oneLiner: Build perpendicular unit vectors from any basis: subtract each new vector's shadow on the ones already fixed, then normalize.
lesson.why: Orthogonal directions decouple computation — projections become dot products, least squares and eigen-decompositions get stable, and conjugate-gradient methods are built on exactly this idea.
lesson.analogy: Straighten a stack of sticks: each new stick loses the part that leans on the already-straightened ones, then gets trimmed to length 1.

steps.text: For each next aₖ subtract its projections: v = aₖ − Σ (aₖ·uⱼ) uⱼ.
If v = 0 the inputs were dependent — stop and drop it.

pitfalls.text: Doing projections against already-normalized vectors vs raw ones changes the formula — with uⱼ unit, the coefficient is just the dot product.
Classical Gram–Schmidt loses orthogonality in floating point; re-run it (or use Householder) when precision matters.

notesGaps: Your notes contain no Gram–Schmidt at all — every line here is labelled [Added by Vertex]
Only the symmetric eigendecomposition A = QΛQᵀ appears, and not how Q is built

trace.title: Gram–Schmidt on a₁=(1,1,0), a₂=(1,0,1)
narration: a₁=(1, 1, 0) only needs normalizing: dividing by √2 gives u₁=(0.7071, 0.7071, 0).
a₂=(1, 0, 1) casts a shadow of 0.7071 on u₁; removing it and normalizing leaves u₂=(0.4082, -0.4082, 0.8165).
trace.takeaway: Subtract every earlier direction's shadow, then normalize — repeat, and you have an orthonormal set spanning the same plane.

lesson.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[next vector a] --> B[dot with each u so far]
  B --> C[a minus those shadows = v]
  C --> D{v is zero?}
  D -- yes --> E[dependent - stop]
  D -- no --> F[u = v / norm]
  F --> G{more vectors?}
  G -- yes --> A
  G -- no --> H[orthonormal basis]

examQuestion.q: Apply Gram–Schmidt to a₁=(1,1,0) and a₂=(0,1,1); give the orthonormal vectors u₁ and u₂. (6 marks)
